rv.q: Beetlejuice the musical is louche, macabre and pure, unadulterated fun, full of black-and-white grotesquerie, visual flair and near-the-knuckle jokes.
The crowd whooped along throughout this mercilessly entertaining celebration of Burton’s madcap ghost caper.
But gradually the thin yet complicated plot begins to stall and sag, and the spiky script, ingenious design and sheer gutsy energy of the cast aren’t enough to compensate.
The numbers are entertaining but oddly unmemorable.
It’s just a shame that a good proportion of the lyrics were lost in the sound mix, at least where I was sitting.
But this undead scene-stealer stops us from taking the actual narrative here seriously; we don’t have space to feel the aching poignancy just beneath its surface.
Ultimately it has nice sets, nice ballads and if you like aggressively knowing 21st century Broadway humour you’ll have fun.
The show has a lot in its favour – not least daft entertainment value – but it lacks essential spark.
Up springs David Fynn’s Beetlejuice straight away, our gratingly eye-popping guide through a story so aimless and scrappy that, before long, you give up even attempting to follow it.
Tightly scripted, tightly choreographed, tightly delivered and for all that, with its great tunes it manages to feel fresh and crisply improvised.
It is, quite simply, dead good.
As a feast for the eyes, the production is utterly spectacular.
It means the show is constantly an amusing ride, but never really flashes its teeth.
Overall, however, it wasn’t a show that emotionally or psychologically connected with me.
Even with all the shiny packaging, Alex Timbers’ production never emotionally flies.
An entertaining night out, but not a memorable one.
If stage musicals, slower, less willing to flood your senses and keener on character development, form your reference point, you’ll be frustrated at the money spent and the opportunities missed.
A gloriously chaotic, visually spectacular triumph - Beetlejuice is the most fun you can have in the afterlife.
Overall, Beetlejuice the Musical is everything you want a musical to be: uproarious and bursting with personality.
Pure entertainment is important in our troubled times and how lucky we are to have a new escape in the West End so overflowing with hilarity, magic and imagination.
Its ear-wormy rock soundtrack is packed with a nice range of teenage angst, laugh-out-loud humour and genuine heart.
Mixed between its bloody & brilliant score, as well as the incredible sets and setpieces, this is an entry the fans do not want to miss out.
Rather than simply recreating the well-loved movie there's a genuine bid to translate its flimsy plot into the language of musical theatre - which makes for a breathlessly enjoyable night out.
Technically brilliant but often overwhelming.
Come for the performances and the spectacle, leave before you start asking whether any of it needed to exist.
Hilarious, heartfelt, and visually bonkers
Death has never been this much fun.
The long-awaited London production of Beetlejuice the Musical ticks all the boxes for a summer night out.

This shows feels that someone has thrown everything into the mix, regardless of the over the top effect of too much comedy, too many sex jokes, too many profanities ignoring a relentless need for some calm and peace.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this loud, visually spectacular Broadway import. While praised for its energetic performances and impressive stagecraft, many find it exhaustingly over-the-top, with relentless humor overshadowing emotional depth.
